body.statement:
At every \(P_0\in\mathcal M_I\) satisfying the displayed constant-rank conditions, profiling \(q_{\mathrm{PT},x}=\delta_1^0(x)\mathbf 1_J-D(x)\) over the unrestricted path of \(\delta_1^0(x)\) yields the observed normal \(R_{\mathrm{PT},x}\) for \(-A_{\mathrm{PT}}D(x)\). Its Gram rank is at most \(J-1\), with equality under positive definiteness on the donor-contrast range. The SC normal Gram rank is at most \(T-J\), with equality under positive definiteness on the residualized complement of \(\operatorname{col}B(x)\). For either branch,
\[
 \mathcal T_b(P_0)=\{s\in\mathcal H_{P_0}:E_{P_{0,O}}[R_{b,x}s]=0\text{ for every }x\in\mathcal X\},
\]
and
\[
 \dot\theta_b(s)=E_{P_{0,O}}\!\left[\left\{\chi_b+\sum_xg^{\circ}_{b,x}\right\}s\right],
 \qquad
 \mathcal I_b(P_0)=\chi_b+\sum_xg^{\circ}_{b,x}+\operatorname{span}\{R_{b,x}:x\in\mathcal X\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \phi_b=\chi_b+\sum_xg^{\circ}_{b,x}
 -R_b^{\prime}\{E_{P_{0,O}}[R_bR_b^{\prime}]\}^{\dagger}
 E_{P_{0,O}}\!\left[R_b\sum_xg^{\circ}_{b,x}\right],
\]
and \(V_b=E_{P_{0,O}}[\chi_b^2]\) plus the minimum variance of the centered branch face. Redundant displayed rows are handled by the Moore--Penrose inverse.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(E_0=E_{P_{0,O}}\). We first profile the PT restriction. By \(\mathrm{def{:}restriction\text{-}maps}\),
\[
 q_{\mathrm{PT},x}=\delta_1^0(x)\mathbf 1_J-D(x),
 \qquad A_{\mathrm{PT}}=I_J-J^{-1}\mathbf 1_J\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Since \(\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}\mathbf 1_J=J\),
\[
 A_{\mathrm{PT}}\mathbf 1_J=0,
 \qquad
 A_{\mathrm{PT}}\dot q_{\mathrm{PT},x}=-A_{\mathrm{PT}}\dot D(x).
 \tag{2}
\]
Thus profiling the unrestricted scalar path \(\dot\delta_1^0(x)\) leaves precisely the observed derivative of \(-A_{\mathrm{PT}}D(x)\). The matrix \(A_{\mathrm{PT}}\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(\{v:\mathbf 1_J^{\prime}v=0\}\), so it has rank \(J-1\). If \(\widetilde R_{D,x}\) represents \(\dot D(x)\), then \(R_{\mathrm{PT},x}=-A_{\mathrm{PT}}\widetilde R_{D,x}\), and hence
\[
 \operatorname{rank}E_0[R_{\mathrm{PT},x}R_{\mathrm{PT},x}^{\prime}]
 \le J-1.
 \tag{3}
\]
Equality holds when the covariance form is positive definite on the range of \(A_{\mathrm{PT}}\), exactly as stated.

For SC put \(\Pi_x=B(x)\{B(x)^{\prime}B(x)\}^{-1}B(x)^{\prime}\). Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}sc\text{-}rank}\) gives an invertible Gram matrix, so \(\Pi_x\) is the orthogonal projector onto the \(J\)-dimensional column space of \(B(x)\). At an SC law \(a(x)=B(x)w(x)\). Differentiating \(\Pi_xB(x)=B(x)\) and then \(r_{\mathrm{SC},x}=(I_T-\Pi_x)a(x)\) gives
\[
 \dot r_{\mathrm{SC},x}
 =(I_T-\Pi_x)\{\dot a(x)-\dot B(x)w(x)\}.
 \tag{4}
\]
Therefore the covariance range of \(R_{\mathrm{SC},x}\) lies in \(\operatorname{range}(I_T-\Pi_x)\), whose dimension is \(T-J\). This proves the SC rank ceiling, and positive definiteness of the residualized covariance form on that range gives equality.

The conditional-residual normalizations used above are available without a new hypothesis. For every occupied cell, quotient differentiation gives
\[
 \dot\mu_{g,t}(x;s)
 =E_0\!\left[
 \frac{\mathbf 1\{G=g,X=x\}}{p_X(x)p_g(x)}
 \{Y_t-\mu_{g,t}(x)\}s\right].
 \tag{5}
\]
The bracketed residual has conditional mean zero given \((G,X)\). Both \(r_{b,x}\) and \(C_b(x)\) are differentiable finite-dimensional functions of these cell means under the displayed rank condition. Applying the ordinary chain rule to (5) therefore constructs versions of \(R_{b,x}\) and \(g^{\circ}_{b,x}\) as linear combinations of such residuals, proving their defining covariance equations and conditional centering.

We next obtain the tangent spaces. The PT observed projection is locally the zero set of \(r_{\mathrm{PT},x}=-A_{\mathrm{PT}}D(x)\): the equality \(A_{\mathrm{PT}}D(x)=0\) is equivalent to \(D(x)=c(x)\mathbf 1_J\), and one can choose the missing treated untreated final mean as \(\mu_{1,T-1}(x)+c(x)\). The SC observed projection is locally the zero set of \(r_{\mathrm{SC},x}=(I_T-\Pi_x)a(x)\): full column rank gives
\[
 r_{\mathrm{SC},x}=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a(x)=B(x)w(x),
 \tag{6}
\]
and the missing treated untreated final mean can be chosen as \(w(x)^{\prime}\mu_{C,T}(x)\). These choices preserve the observed law and impose the corresponding full-data restriction. No anticipation justifies using observed preperiod and donor means in both constructions; overlap makes every conditional mean well defined.

Differentiating the branch equations along a branch-preserving path gives
\[
 E_0[R_{b,x}s]=0\quad\text{for every }x.
 \tag{7}
\]
Conversely, retain a maximal linearly independent coordinate vector \(R_b^{*}\). Constant rank permits the same coordinate choice locally. Its Gram matrix is positive definite. Truncating and recentering its coordinates produces a bounded vector \(v\) for which \(M=E_0[R_b^{*}v^{\prime}]\) is nonsingular. For a bounded, mean-zero score \(s\) satisfying (7), use the exponential tilt
\[
 \frac{dP_{O,\varepsilon,c}}{dP_{0,O}}
 =\frac{\exp\{\varepsilon s+c^{\prime}v\}}
 {E_0[\exp\{\varepsilon s+c^{\prime}v\}]},
 \qquad F(\varepsilon,c)=r_b^{*}(P_{O,\varepsilon,c}).
 \tag{8}
\]
Finite support, overlap, bounded tilting directions, and the fourth-moment condition justify differentiation of the conditional means. At the origin,
\[
 F(0,0)=0,
 \qquad \partial_cF(0,0)=M,
 \qquad \partial_{\varepsilon}F(0,0)=E_0[R_b^{*}s]=0.
 \tag{9}
\]
We derive the correction directly. Differentiability and (9) give
\[
 F(\varepsilon,c)=F(\varepsilon,0)+Mc+\zeta(\varepsilon,c),
 \qquad F(\varepsilon,0)=o(\varepsilon),
\]
where, on a sufficiently small ball, the Lipschitz constant of \(c\mapsto M^{-1}\zeta(\varepsilon,c)\) is at most \(1/2\). Hence
\[
 \mathcal K_\varepsilon(c)=-M^{-1}\{F(\varepsilon,0)+\zeta(\varepsilon,c)\}
\]
maps a ball of radius \(C|\varepsilon|\) into itself and is a contraction for a fixed sufficiently large \(C\). Starting from zero, its iterates satisfy \(\|c_{j+1}-c_j\|\le2^{-j}\|c_1-c_0\|\), so they are Cauchy and converge in finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Continuity makes the limit \(c(\varepsilon)\) a fixed point. Thus \(F(\varepsilon,c(\varepsilon))=0\), and \(F(\varepsilon,0)=o(\varepsilon)\) gives \(c(\varepsilon)=o(\varepsilon)\). The corrected path has score \(s\). The full-data extensions above lift it into branch \(b\). For a general square-integrable \(s\), truncate and recenter to \(\widetilde s_k\), and set
\[
 s_k=\widetilde s_k-v^{\prime}M^{-1}E_0[R_b^{*}\widetilde s_k].
 \tag{10}
\]
Then \(E_0[R_b^{*}s_k]=0\) and \(s_k\to s\) in \(L^2(P_{0,O})\). Taking the closure specified in \(\mathrm{def{:}branch\text{-}tangents}\) proves
\[
 \mathcal T_b(P_0)=\{s\in\mathcal H_{P_0}:E_0[R_{b,x}s]=0\text{ for all }x\}.
 \tag{11}
\]

It remains to restore the product-rule term omitted by the old formula. Put \(q_x=P_O(G=1,X=x)\). Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}cell\text{-}mass}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}group\text{-}overlap}\) imply \(\pi_1=\sum_xq_x>0\). Along an arbitrary observed-data score \(s\), quotient differentiation of \(\nu_x=q_x/\pi_1\) yields
\[
 \dot\nu_x(s)
 =E_0\!\left[\frac{\mathbf 1\{G=1\}}{\pi_1}
 \{\mathbf 1\{X=x\}-\nu_x\}s\right].
 \tag{12}
\]
Since \(\theta_b=\sum_x\nu_xC_b(x)\), equation (12) and \(\mathrm{def{:}normal\text{-}gradients}\) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \dot\theta_b(s)
 &=\sum_x C_b(x)\dot\nu_x(s)+\sum_x\nu_x\dot C_b(x;s)\\
 &=E_0[\chi_b s]+\sum_xE_0[g^{\circ}_{b,x}s]
 =E_0\!\left[\left\{\chi_b+\sum_xg^{\circ}_{b,x}\right\}s\right].
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{13}
\]
This proves the derivative identity rather than building it into the causal target.

There are finitely many retained normals, so (11) implies \(\mathcal T_b(P_0)^{\perp}=\operatorname{span}\{R_{b,x}:x\in\mathcal X\}\). Combining this with (13) and \(\mathrm{def{:}influence\text{-}classes}\) gives
\[
 \mathcal I_b(P_0)=\chi_b+\sum_xg^{\circ}_{b,x}
 +\operatorname{span}\{R_{b,x}:x\in\mathcal X\}.
 \tag{14}
\]
The conditional-residual normalization gives \(E_0[R_{b,x}\mid G,X]=0\), whereas \(\chi_b\) is measurable with respect to \((G,X)\); hence \(E_0[R_b\chi_b]=0\). Let \(G_b^{\circ}=\sum_xg^{\circ}_{b,x}\), \(\Gamma_b=E_0[R_bR_b^{\prime}]\), and \(u_b=E_0[R_bG_b^{\circ}]\). If \(c\in\ker\Gamma_b\), then \(c^{\prime}R_b=0\) almost surely, so \(c^{\prime}u_b=0\); thus \(u_b\in\operatorname{range}\Gamma_b\). Completing the square yields
\[
 \|\chi_b+G_b^{\circ}+R_b^{\prime}a\|_2^2
 =\|\chi_b+G_b^{\circ}-R_b^{\prime}\Gamma_b^{\dagger}u_b\|_2^2
 +(a+\Gamma_b^{\dagger}u_b)^{\prime}\Gamma_b(a+\Gamma_b^{\dagger}u_b).
 \tag{15}
\]
Minimizing (15) proves the displayed canonical-gradient formula. Moreover \(E_0[\chi_b g^{\circ}_{b,x}]=0\) by the same conditional-residual argument, so its variance is \(E_0[\chi_b^2]\) plus the minimized centered-face variance. This completes every asserted rank, tangent, influence-class, and variance statement.
body.justification: This places both corrected branch faces in one observed-data Hilbert space, separates the common treated-composition derivative from centered conditional-mean derivatives, and records the PT and SC rank ceilings.
body.gap: Existing branchwise results do not jointly characterize the two affine classes with the product-rule composition term and both profiled normal ranks.
body.consumer: For the Alaska design, this supplies the geometry needed to calculate a theoretical union lower-bound benchmark; it does not supply a standard error.
